# Why now

> My average position for October is 14, but the SEO team reports 6. Is there a mistake in the data?
> — A colleague from marketing, preparing the month report

There is none: both figures come from the same rows, and both look like a position. Only one of them is the position of the site, and the SEO team knew which; they had explained it to one colleague at a time.

Promise: what a pitfall of a Resource is, and why it belongs on its card.

# Core idea

A **pitfall** is a way to read a table wrongly that looks right: written on its card, the next colleague steps around it.

## At Immoscoop

Search Console impressions, whole site, in the Collection Attraction, holds how often the site appears in Google and at which position, in one row per day, query, country, device and search type. Every row is right, yet the average of their positions is not the position of the site: it gives a row with ten impressions as much weight as one with ten thousand, where Google weighs each row by its impressions. So the SEO team, its Owner, writes it among its pitfalls: "Do not average the position: weigh each row by its impressions." From then on it stands under Known Behaviour on the Overview of the Resource, and Claude reads it too. Nothing is missing, so it is not a Known Gap: the data is right, and the reading goes wrong.

# Check your understanding

## A Resource holds leads per week and per lead source. A colleague adds up the sources to count the leads of a week, and a lead that came in through two sources counts twice. What is that?

- [ ] A bug: the Data Team should fix the table
- [ ] A Known Gap: part of the data is missing
- [x] A pitfall: every row is right, and adding them up reads them wrong

Why: one lead in two sources is two rows, as the table promises, so there is nothing to fix and nothing missing. The mistake is in the reading, and the total looks right: that is what a pitfall warns of.

## Under Known Behaviour, the pitfalls of a Resource you want to use say "Nothing written yet." What does that tell you?

- [ ] It has no pitfalls
- [ ] The Data Team checked it and found none
- [x] Nobody wrote any, nor said there are none: ask its Owner before you trust a figure that matters

Why: silence is not an answer, as nobody may have looked. When its Owner or the Data Team says there are none, the card says so: "None, according to" whom, on which day.

## Your team owns a Resource. In a chat, you explained to a colleague why a figure they took from it was wrong. What now?

- [ ] Nothing more: they know now
- [ ] Wait until a second colleague makes the same mistake, to be sure it is worth writing down
- [x] Write it among the pitfalls of the Resource, so that the next colleague reads it before making the same mistake

Why: a chat reaches one colleague, once. Written among the pitfalls, it reaches everyone who opens the Resource, and Claude reads it too; waiting for the second mistake means someone makes it.

# You can now

read the pitfalls of a Resource before you trust a figure from it, and ask "what trips people up with this table?" before you publish a Resource of your own.
